finding: A command-line tool that turns each title line on standard input into a URL slug on standard output (lower-case words joined by hyphens) drops letters outside the Latin alphabet instead of keeping them. On 2 Greek titles holding 10 letters, it kept 0 of the 10 letters: "Ωμέγα" gave an empty line and "Δέλτα 4" gave "4", where the tool's specification expects "ωμεγα" and "δελτα-4". A filter meant to remove punctuation and spaces must decide by whether a character is a letter or a digit in any script, not by membership in one alphabet.
reference: The tool's specification, in its use case on letters outside the Latin alphabet, gives the expected output for this input as the two lines "ωμεγα" and "δελτα-4": every letter kept, lower-cased and without its accent.

pattern.context: A text tool keeps some characters and drops the rest, for instance to build a URL slug from a title, and its input can contain letters of any script.
pattern.problem: The keep rule names one alphabet (such as a to z) instead of the class "letter or digit", so every letter of another script is dropped as if it were punctuation: on 2 Greek titles with 10 letters, 0 letters survived, one title became an empty line and the other became only its digit.
pattern.solution: Keep a character when it is a letter or a digit in any script; lower-case it and remove its accent, and drop only what is neither letter nor digit. The 2 titles then give "ωμεγα" and "δελτα-4".
pattern.consequences: With the fault, titles in other scripts lose all their words and silently collapse to empty or digit-only output, so distinct titles collide; no error is raised. With the solution, every script keeps its words, at the cost of slugs that are no longer plain ASCII.
